\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_temperature_robustness}
\caption{Temperature robustness on SciERC ($N{=}8$). Top: NER; bottom: RE. SJ maintains stable $\rho$ across $T{=}0.7$ and $T{=}1.0$, while FK shows mixed sensitivity. LP $T{=}0.7$ data unavailable.}
\label{fig:temperature_robustness}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Temperature sensitivity.}
SJ NER $\rho$ shifts from 0.388 ($T{=}0.7$) to 0.360 ($T{=}1.0$), a difference of 0.028 whose bootstrap confidence interval includes zero.
FK shows mixed behavior: NER $\rho$ drops by 0.054, while RE $\rho$ increases by 0.091, likely reflecting reduced diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks.
Across all comparisons, the SJ--FK relative ordering is preserved at both temperatures on NER (0.388 vs.\ 0.321 at $T{=}0.7$; 0.360 vs.\ 0.267 at $T{=}1.0$), indicating a stable signal hierarchy despite numerically small temperature effects.

\paragraph{Sample size scaling.}
Increasing from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ improves SJ on Qwen SciERC NER: $\rho$ rises from 0.360 to $0.412{\pm}0.025$ (three seeds: 0.428, 0.424, 0.384), a gain of $+0.052$.
The magnitude of $N$-scaling gains is setting-dependent---LLaMA SciERC NER yields $+0.016$ and Qwen CoNLL NER $+0.014$---though the direction is consistently positive.
LLaMA CoNLL exhibits the most uniform scaling: all four consistency signals gain $\Delta\rho{\approx}{+}0.030$ (range: $+0.027$ to $+0.032$) while LP gains only $+0.003$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}).
FK $N$-scaling is inconsistent: degradation on SciERC ($-0.007$ to $-0.019$) but improvement on CoNLL with LLaMA ($+0.027$), suggesting sensitivity to both model and task characteristics.
VC $N$-scaling is consistently positive ($+0.005$ on Qwen CoNLL, $+0.018$ on LLaMA SciERC, $+0.062$ on Qwen SciERC), while LP is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta{\leq}0.021$).
SJ, EM, and voting confidence scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows setting-dependent variation, suggesting that structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to $N$.

\paragraph{Cross-model transfer.}
LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct replicates the structural-over-surface ordering on SciERC NER (SJ $\rho{=}0.363$, FK $\rho{=}0.327$).
On CoNLL, the gap across model families is minimal (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA) vs.\ 0.436 (Qwen), $\Delta{=}0.005$.
At $N{=}16$, the structural-over-LP advantage holds across all four tested settings: Qwen SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.411$ vs.\ LP 0.259, $\Delta{=}{+}0.152$), Qwen CoNLL (EM $\rho{=}0.463$ vs.\ LP 0.328, $\Delta{=}{+}0.135$), LLaMA SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.452$ vs.\ LP 0.277, $\Delta{=}{+}0.175$), and LLaMA CoNLL 3-seed (SJ $\rho{=}0.463{\pm}0.007$ vs.\ LP $0.310{\pm}0.005$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.153$).

NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069--0.096), while RE shows greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339), reflecting the difficulty of calibrating confidence for compound extraction tasks.}

NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069--0.096), while RE exhibits greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339), indicating that translating consistency scores into calibrated confidence estimates is feasible for NER but remains challenging for compound extraction tasks.

\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
The SJ advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: VC reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, LP $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.

\paragraph{Length vs.\ log-probability.}
Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter} shows that mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$, $n{=}4{,}232$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$, $n{=}3{,}176$), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for LP's selection failure: longer outputs receive \textit{higher}, not lower, token-averaged log-probability under constrained decoding.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_length_logprob_scatter}
\caption{Output length vs.\ mean log-probability on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Positive correlations (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$) rule out length-penalty confounding.}
\label{fig:length_logprob_scatter}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, making the two selection rules equivalent.
Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, confirming that structural advantage is robust across both models and evaluation conditions.
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while LP drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

\paragraph{WNUT-17 full signal analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:wnut} reports all five signals on WNUT-17.
VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$) on the full set, but conditional analysis (non-zero F1 instances) reveals this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary: conditional $\rho{=}0.038$ ($p{=}0.49$).
LP shows the reverse pattern: full-set $\rho{=}{-}0.410$ but conditional $\rho{=}0.350$, the highest among all signals on the conditional set.
This inversion confirms that full-set correlations on high-failure-rate datasets conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.

Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection} extends the selection analysis to four additional configurations.
On LLaMA SciERC, where output diversity remains substantial (18\% identical outputs, 39\% unique), LP achieves the highest selection F1 (0.652) at $N{=}8$ but still falls within bootstrap noise of greedy (0.646), replicating the gap observed on Qwen SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
On CoNLL, 57--88\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples, reflecting a ceiling effect (greedy F1 ${\approx}$0.91--0.92) rather than signal failure; selection analysis on these configurations is uninformative because there is little per-sample variance for any signal to exploit.

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2024scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.052$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.153$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\section{Bootstrap CI for Signal Comparisons}\label{app:bootstrap_signal}

Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap_signal_ci} reports bootstrap confidence intervals for individual signal $\rho$ and pairwise $\Delta\rho$ on SciERC NER ($N{=}8$, $n{=}529$, $B{=}10{,}000$, seed${=}42$).
The SJ--LP gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$) is clearly significant, confirming the structural advantage reported in \S\ref{sec:qe_results}.
The VC--SJ gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.019$) is not significant, indicating that these two structural signals perform comparably.
The SJ--EM gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.065$) is borderline significant, with the CI lower bound at $+0.003$ and upper bound at $+0.130$.

\section{Diversity and Selection Analysis}\label{app:diversity}

\paragraph{Output diversity quantification.}
Table~\ref{tab:diversity} summarizes output diversity across configurations.
On SciERC, output diversity is substantial: Qwen produces 43\% unique outputs per instance (mean 3.5 distinct out of $N{=}8$), with per-sample F1 standard deviation of 0.144 and mean pairwise SJ of 0.703.
LLaMA shows similar diversity (39\% unique, F1 std 0.11).
On CoNLL, diversity collapses: 57\% (Qwen) to 88\% (LLaMA) of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples, reflecting a ceiling effect where greedy F1 already exceeds 0.90.
WNUT-17 shows 55\% identical outputs, driven by the 52\% zero-F1 rate.

\paragraph{Oracle-improvable fraction.}
Across SciERC configurations, 39--42\% of instances contain at least one sample with F1 exceeding greedy: Qwen NER 42.0\% (222/529, mean headroom $+$31.9~pp among improvable instances), Qwen RE 41.3\% (164/397, $+$45.3~pp), LLaMA NER 39.3\% (208/529, $+$33.7~pp).
On CoNLL, only 4--9\% of instances are improvable, confirming the ceiling effect.

\paragraph{Diversity-stratified selection gap.}
On the 44\% of Qwen SciERC instances with high diversity (${\geq}4$ unique outputs among 8 samples, $n{=}232$), oracle headroom reaches $+$16.3~pp, yet all consistency-based signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) select at or below greedy, and LP---the only per-sample signal---achieves merely $+$0.8~pp.
LLaMA replicates this pattern: on its high-diversity subset ($n{=}186$), oracle headroom reaches $+$20.1~pp while consistency signals remain at or below greedy and LP captures only $+$2.0~pp.
This rules out insufficient diversity as an explanation for the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}
The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to greedy within a bound $\delta$.
The $\delta$ values are anchored to oracle headroom (13--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
\texttt{[PENDING: breakpoint $\delta^*$ ranges from X to Y~pp across configurations.]}
On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to greedy (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

\paragraph{Prompt template.}
For NER, we use a structured prompt:
\begin{quote}
\small
\texttt{System:} You are an expert in Named Entity Recognition.\\
\texttt{User:} Extract all named entities from the following text. Output as JSON.\\
Text: \texttt{\{input\_text\}}\\
Entity types: \texttt{\{schema\_types\}}
\end{quote}
RE follows the same structure with ``Relation Extraction'' and relation type lists substituted accordingly.

\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar-based JSON schema enforcement \cite{willard2023guided}, which constrains outputs to valid entity/relation structures matching the target schema.
This eliminates format errors but may compress per-sample diversity by restricting the output space.\footnote{SciERC training did not explicitly disable thinking tokens (\texttt{enable\_thinking}); CoNLL and WNUT explicitly set this to false. Constrained decoding at inference time overrides any thinking behavior by enforcing JSON-only output.}

\section{Log-Probability Score Compression}\label{app:logprob_ties}

Under constrained decoding, log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, limiting per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}).
The median within-instance LP range is only 0.041, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$).
At $\varepsilon{=}0.05$, 60.3\% of instances have a within-sample range below the threshold, leaving LP unable to meaningfully distinguish candidates.
For comparison, SJ has only 12.5\% tied instances at the same threshold---SJ's advantage over LP for selection is one of score resolution, not information content.

\paragraph{Non-tied subset.}
Among instances with LP range ${\geq}0.05$ ($n{=}210$, 40\% of total), log-probability selection \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp F1, $p{=}0.01$), and within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied subset).
This confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information but is resolution-limited under constrained decoding---the signal exists but is compressed below the discrimination threshold for most instances.

\section{RE Conditional Selection}\label{app:re_conditional_selection}

Table~\ref{tab:re_cond_selection} extends the selection analysis to the RE non-zero F1 subset.
Of $n{=}397$ RE instances, 238 (60\%) have non-zero F1 and 159 (40\%) have zero F1.
All five signals underperform greedy on both subsets.
On the non-zero subset, selection performance is \textit{worse} than on the full set (e.g., VC: $-10.0$~pp on non-zero vs.\ $-4.5$~pp on full set), because greedy is already strong on non-zero instances (F1${=}0.674$) and signals actively select inferior samples.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2024scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
These require fundamentally different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
The most relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE, finding results that our quality-estimation analysis corroborates.
Our work extends theirs in three directions: (i)~structural matching beyond surface-level agreement, (ii)~testing whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection (it does not), and (iii)~a difficulty gradient revealing non-obvious findings---WNUT-17 conditional correlations collapse to $\rho{=}0.038$ (n.s.) and LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$)---that would be invisible on a single dataset.

Structured IE requires schema-compliant output, making constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} the standard inference strategy---without it, a substantial fraction of outputs are unparseable.
All experiments use constrained decoding, the regime under which structured IE is practically deployed.

Our central finding is the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): under constrained decoding, consistency-based signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) but fail at sample selection despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
By construction, four of five signals assign identical scores to all candidates from the same input, precluding per-sample discrimination.
The non-trivial questions are whether (a)~consensus-proximity selection---instantiating MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, freitag2022high, muller2021understanding} with structural utility functions---can recover discrimination, and (b)~whether log-probability, the only per-sample signal, can exploit the headroom.
Both fail: MBR utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); log-probability is severely compressed under constrained decoding (60\% of instances effectively tied), though where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
Our findings are specific to the constrained decoding regime; whether the gap persists under free-form generation remains an open question.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals predict instance-level quality---high agreement correlates with high F1. \textbf{Right}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, precluding sample selection. Consensus-proximity selection does not recover per-sample discrimination.}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting confidence [VC], Soft Jaccard [SJ]), surface (exact match [EM], Fleiss' $\kappa$ [FK]), and model-internal (log-probability [LP])---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.
Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{The correlation-selection gap and its mechanistic diagnosis.}
    We demonstrate that strong quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$, AUROC${=}0.75$) coexists with selection failure ($p{>}0.39$, 13--18~pp oracle headroom) under constrained decoding.
    Log-probability---the only per-sample signal---fails due to constrained-decoding-induced score compression (60\% of instances effectively tied); where compression is mitigated, it becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
    MBR decoding with structural utility functions also fails, as utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them.

    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
    Signal rankings shift with task difficulty: EM leads on easy tasks, SJ on hard tasks---consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
    At the capability boundary (WNUT-17, 52\% zero F1), conditional correlations collapse to non-significance and LP exhibits strong negative correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$), indicating overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs.
    NER findings span three datasets; RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone (preliminary).
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
4	For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though exact match leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
5	Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across tested model families, though with model-dependent magnitude.
6	When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
7	
8	\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
9	\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
10	Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
11	\textit{Layer 2 (constrained-decoding compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
12	Under constrained decoding, LP scores are severely compressed: 60\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
13	In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
14	This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---is the primary mechanistic bottleneck, though whether compression fully accounts for the gap remains open.
15	The LP compression mechanism is a direct consequence of constrained decoding's restricted token space; alternative decoding strategies may yield different LP distributions.
16	Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.
17	
18	\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
19	Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
20	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
21	\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.
22	
23	\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
24	The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
25	Effective selection likely requires either per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust} or relaxation of the constrained-decoding regime that compresses LP resolution; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though exact match leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across tested model families, though with model-dependent magnitude.
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (constrained-decoding compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
Under constrained decoding, LP scores are severely compressed: 60\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---is the primary mechanistic bottleneck, though whether compression fully accounts for the gap remains open.
The LP compression mechanism is a direct consequence of constrained decoding's restricted token space; alternative decoding strategies may yield different LP distributions.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires either per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust} or relaxation of the constrained-decoding regime that compresses LP resolution; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.

84	\label{sec:selection_gap}
85	
86	\begin{figure*}[t]
87	\centering
88	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_selection_gap}
89	\caption{The correlation-selection gap on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Left: NER; right: RE. Bars show best-of-$N$ selection F1; the line marks quality estimation $\rho$. Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal significantly outperforms greedy on either task ($p{=}0.39$ for NER LP, the best signal; Table~\ref{tab:selection}). Dashed line indicates oracle upper bound.}
90	\label{fig:selection_gap}
91	\end{figure*}
92	
93	\begin{table}[t]
94	\centering
95	\small
96	\caption{Best-of-$N$ selection F1 on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). RE results are from a single benchmark (preliminary). Best non-oracle result per column in \textbf{bold}. EM selects the plurality output; despite a 42\% pairwise exact-match rate, EM selection underperforms greedy on both tasks.}
97	\label{tab:selection}
98	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
99	\toprule
100	Method & NER F1 & RE F1 \\
101	\midrule
102	Oracle & 0.776 & 0.585 \\
103	\midrule
104	LP           & \textbf{0.650} & 0.395 \\
105	SJ       & 0.645 & 0.386 \\
106	EM        & 0.636 & 0.372 \\
107	VC                 & 0.634 & 0.359 \\
108	\midrule
109	Greedy ($T{=}0$)   & 0.644 & \textbf{0.404} \\
110	Random             & 0.608 & 0.354 \\
111	\bottomrule
112	\end{tabular}
113	\end{table}

115	Despite strong quality estimation, confidence signals yield limited gains when used for best-of-$N$ selection (Table~\ref{tab:selection}, Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}).
116	Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input regardless of which sample is evaluated; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
117	The non-trivial question is whether log-probability---the only per-sample signal---can exploit the oracle headroom.
118	We anchor this analysis on SciERC, where output diversity is substantial: only 11--18\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N{=}8$ samples, with 39--43\% unique outputs per instance (mean 3.5 distinct outputs), per-sample F1 standard deviation of 0.11--0.14, and mean pairwise SJ of 0.703.
119	
120	\paragraph{No significant improvement over greedy.}
121	We exclude 22 instances with empty gold annotations ($n{=}529$) and evaluate significance via instance-level paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$).
122	On NER, the oracle (0.776) reveals 13.2~pp of headroom above greedy (0.644).
123	LP achieves the highest selection F1 (0.650, +0.6~pp), but this is not significant ($p{=}0.39$; 95\% CI: [$-$3.0, +4.2]~pp; Cohen's $d{=}0.038$).
124	On RE, the best signal (LP, 0.395) falls below greedy (0.404, $-0.9$\,pp, $p{=}0.80$), while 18.1~pp of oracle headroom remains.
125	TOST equivalence testing confirms most signals are indistinguishable from greedy at ${\pm}2$--$3$~pp on NER; on RE, EM and VC fail equivalence even at ${\pm}5$~pp (Table~\ref{tab:tost}, Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).
126	VC ($\rho{=}0.379$, the best quality estimator) selects to only 0.634 on NER---\textit{below} greedy.
127	The gap extends to CoNLL (ceiling effect, 57--88\% identical outputs) and WNUT-17 (capability boundary; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
128	
129	\paragraph{Quality estimation $\neq$ output selection.}
130	Instance-level confidence signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} among $N$ candidates is best.
131	When per-sample variance is low relative to instance-level difficulty, even perfect quality estimation cannot discriminate among near-identical candidates.
132	This gap has direct consequences for test-time scaling in IE \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2024scaling}: closing it likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}.

135	\subsection{Robustness}
136	\label{sec:robustness_main}
137	
138	Consistency-based signals show robust performance across $T{\in}\{0.7, 1.0\}$ (SJ NER $\Delta\rho{=}0.028$, bootstrap CI includes zero) and sublinear gains from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, with structural signals maintaining their advantage over LP across all settings ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.135$ to ${+}0.175$; Table~\ref{tab:robustness}, Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).

2	
3	Within the constrained decoding regime standard for structured IE, we demonstrate that consistency signals are effective quality estimators ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) but fail at sample selection---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Within the constrained decoding regime standard for structured IE, we demonstrate that consistency signals are effective quality estimators ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) but fail at sample selection---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
By construction, four of five signals assign identical scores to all candidates from the same input; log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails ($p{>}0.39$) despite 13--18~pp oracle headroom due to constrained-decoding-induced score compression.
Where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$); consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) similarly fails as utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty, with consistent ordering across two model families at 8B scale.
RE findings rest on SciERC alone (preliminary, single benchmark) and warrant multi-benchmark validation.
Trained verifiers, relaxed decoding constraints, scaling to 70B+ models, and conformal prediction are promising directions.

Our evaluation covers three datasets but only one RE benchmark (SciERC), where 40\% of instances receive zero F1, compressing the discriminable range and limiting signal differentiation for relation extraction.
RE selection failure persists even when restricting to non-zero F1 instances (Appendix~\ref{app:re_conditional_selection}), ruling out floor effects as the sole explanation, but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
WNUT-17 confirms the capability boundary of our approach, but our positive results on formal-domain text (CoNLL, SciERC) have not been validated on informal or noisy text where models achieve non-trivial performance.

We evaluate two model families (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B), both at 8B parameters.
A 3-seed robustness analysis confirms that signal rankings are stable across seeds ($\sigma{\leq}0.025$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), but whether our findings---particularly the correlation-selection gap and the difficulty-dependent signal ordering---hold for larger models (70B+) or closed-source APIs remains untested.
Larger models may produce higher-quality and more diverse samples, potentially altering the signal landscape.

Our analysis of selection potential uses only unsupervised signals.
We do not train a dedicated verifier or reward model, leaving unknown how much of the oracle headroom a supervised approach could recover.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$.
The behavior of confidence signals at larger sample sizes (e.g., $N{=}64$ or $N{=}128$) is unknown, and $N$-scaling gains are setting-dependent: SJ improves by $+0.052$ on Qwen SciERC NER but only $+0.016$ on LLaMA SciERC NER when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$.

On CoNLL with LLaMA, the SJ--FK gap is only 0.003 ($\rho{=}0.431$ vs.\ $0.428$), so the structural advantage over surface signals may not generalize to all simple-schema datasets.
Constrained decoding (Outlines/vLLM) enforces schema compliance, potentially compressing per-sample diversity and contributing to the correlation-selection gap beyond what free-form generation would exhibit.
Our non-tied subset analysis (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests this compression is the primary driver---quantifying the gap under free-form generation is an important open question.

Qwen3-8B supports a thinking mode (\texttt{enable\_thinking}), which was not explicitly disabled during SciERC training (it was disabled for CoNLL and WNUT).
At inference time, constrained decoding overrides any thinking behavior by enforcing JSON-only output, so thinking tokens do not appear in generated samples.
However, exposure to thinking tokens during training may affect learned representations, introducing a minor inconsistency between the SciERC and CoNLL/WNUT training configurations.

Finally, log-probability was excluded from the temperature comparison ($T{=}0.7$ vs.\ $T{=}1.0$) due to missing $T{=}0.7$ LP data, leaving its temperature sensitivity uncharacterized.

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
2	
3	\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
4	Self-consistency decoding \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning by majority voting over chain-of-thought samples, assuming a discrete answer space.
5	Extensions to free-form text use LLM-based comparison \cite{chen2024usc}, atomic sub-claim decomposition \cite{thirukovalluru2024atomic}, or cross-sample hallucination detection \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
6	For test-time scaling \cite{zhang2025tts}, \citet{snell2024scaling} characterize compute scaling laws and \citet{brown2024monkeys} show best-of-$N$ gains across tasks.
7	Recent reward-free selectors include confidence-weighted voting \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc}, KL-based self-certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty}, adaptive sampling \cite{kim2026reasc}, ranked aggregation \cite{wang2025rankedvoting}, and latent-space consistency \cite{oh2025latentsc}.
8	Concurrently, \citet{feng2025optimal} and \citet{wang2025make} adapt self-consistency to difficulty-aware settings, echoing our finding that signal rankings shift with task complexity; \citet{li2025llms} propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on output fusion rather than confidence-based selection.
9	All of the above target reasoning/QA with discrete answers or specific aggregation strategies.
10	Our work extends self-consistency to set-valued structured outputs and identifies the correlation-selection gap: strong quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$) coexists with selection failure ($p{>}0.39$).
11	
12	\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
13	\citet{nedellec2026consistency} study consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based NER/RE, corroborating our quality-estimation findings.
14	Their work leaves open three questions we address: (i)~whether structural matching improves on surface-level agreement (which they acknowledge ``overlooks semantically consistent outputs''); (ii)~whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection; and (iii)~whether findings generalize across a difficulty gradient.
15	Our Soft Jaccard signal addresses (i) through type-aware bipartite matching with token-level span overlap; our selection analysis (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}) directly addresses (ii); and our three-dataset evaluation spanning easy (CoNLL) to hard (SciERC) tasks addresses (iii).
16	CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses model confidence with inter-sample consistency for QA/summarization but does not address structured extraction.
17	Our evaluation builds on generative IE work \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, josifoski2022genie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, wang2023instructuie} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.
18	
19	\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and calibration.}
20	Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, selective abstention \cite{wen2025know}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic} for LLMs; \citet{xiong2024llm} find LLMs tend toward overconfidence, and \citet{heo2025uncertainty} show calibration degrades with task complexity.
21	Semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} clusters generations by meaning; \citet{kossen2024semantic} distill this into probes; P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} queries model confidence directly; \citet{malinin2021uncertainty} distinguish data and model uncertainty in autoregressive models.
22	Our structural signals instead measure agreement over output \textit{structure}.
23	Neural networks are often miscalibrated \cite{guo2017calibration, desai2020calibration}; deep ensembles \cite{lakshminarayanan2017ensembles} and MC-dropout \cite{gal2016dropout} obtain uncertainty from model variation, while our approach requires no model modification.
24	Prior NER and sequence-labeling uncertainty work \cite{xiao2019uncertainty, shelmanov2021active, zhang2023ener, kim2024verifiner, he2024uncertainty} operates within discriminative, verification, or transmission-based paradigms.
25	Conformal prediction \cite{fisch2021conformal, angelopoulos2021conformal} provides coverage guarantees; trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, venktesh2025trust} and reward models \cite{wang2024mathshepherd} learn per-sample scoring.
26	Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling} with structural utility functions; despite MBR's success in translation \cite{freitag2022high} and other generation tasks \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, we find utility-quality misalignment at the per-sample level for structured IE (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
27	Selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective} and confidence-based IE filtering \cite{culotta2004confidence} establish the broader framework.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency decoding \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning by majority voting over chain-of-thought samples, assuming a discrete answer space.
Extensions to free-form text use LLM-based comparison \cite{chen2024usc}, atomic sub-claim decomposition \cite{thirukovalluru2024atomic}, or cross-sample hallucination detection \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
For test-time scaling \cite{zhang2025tts}, \citet{snell2024scaling} characterize compute scaling laws and \citet{brown2024monkeys} show best-of-$N$ gains across tasks.
Recent reward-free selectors include confidence-weighted voting \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc}, KL-based self-certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty}, adaptive sampling \cite{kim2026reasc}, ranked aggregation \cite{wang2025rankedvoting}, and latent-space consistency \cite{oh2025latentsc}.
Concurrently, \citet{feng2025optimal} and \citet{wang2025make} adapt self-consistency to difficulty-aware settings, echoing our finding that signal rankings shift with task complexity; \citet{li2025llms} propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on output fusion rather than confidence-based selection.
All of the above target reasoning/QA with discrete answers or specific aggregation strategies.
Our work extends self-consistency to set-valued structured outputs and identifies the correlation-selection gap: strong quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$) coexists with selection failure ($p{>}0.39$).

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{nedellec2026consistency} study consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based NER/RE, corroborating our quality-estimation findings.
Their work leaves open three questions we address: (i)~whether structural matching improves on surface-level agreement (which they acknowledge ``overlooks semantically consistent outputs''); (ii)~whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection; and (iii)~whether findings generalize across a difficulty gradient.
Our Soft Jaccard signal addresses (i) through type-aware bipartite matching with token-level span overlap; our selection analysis (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}) directly addresses (ii); and our three-dataset evaluation spanning easy (CoNLL) to hard (SciERC) tasks addresses (iii).
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses model confidence with inter-sample consistency for QA/summarization but does not address structured extraction.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE work \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, josifoski2022genie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, wang2023instructuie} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and calibration.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, selective abstention \cite{wen2025know}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic} for LLMs; \citet{xiong2024llm} find LLMs tend toward overconfidence, and \citet{heo2025uncertainty} show calibration degrades with task complexity.
Semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} clusters generations by meaning; \citet{kossen2024semantic} distill this into probes; P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} queries model confidence directly; \citet{malinin2021uncertainty} distinguish data and model uncertainty in autoregressive models.
Our structural signals instead measure agreement over output \textit{structure}.
Neural networks are often miscalibrated \cite{guo2017calibration, desai2020calibration}; deep ensembles \cite{lakshminarayanan2017ensembles} and MC-dropout \cite{gal2016dropout} obtain uncertainty from model variation, while our approach requires no model modification.
Prior NER and sequence-labeling uncertainty work \cite{xiao2019uncertainty, shelmanov2021active, zhang2023ener, kim2024verifiner, he2024uncertainty} operates within discriminative, verification, or transmission-based paradigms.
Conformal prediction \cite{fisch2021conformal, angelopoulos2021conformal} provides coverage guarantees; trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, venktesh2025trust} and reward models \cite{wang2024mathshepherd} learn per-sample scoring.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling} with structural utility functions; despite MBR's success in translation \cite{freitag2022high} and other generation tasks \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, we find utility-quality misalignment at the per-sample level for structured IE (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective} and confidence-based IE filtering \cite{culotta2004confidence} establish the broader framework.

\begin{abstract}
Test-time scaling through repeated sampling promises quality gains for LLM-based information extraction (IE), but whether confidence signals can identify the best among multiple outputs remains untested for structured tasks.
Under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---we compare five confidence signals across NER and RE with two 8B-parameter model families.
These signals achieve strong quality estimation (Spearman $\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75), yet none significantly improves sample selection over greedy decoding despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom---a \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
By construction, four of five signals assign identical scores to all candidates from the same input, precluding per-sample selection.
The remaining signal---log-probability---fails because constrained decoding compresses its scores (60\% of instances effectively tied), but becomes a significant selector where compression is mitigated ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
Consensus-proximity selection, instantiating minimum Bayes risk decoding, similarly fails because utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
These results establish that consistency signals are quality estimators, not output selectors, for structured IE under constrained decoding.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2024scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
These require fundamentally different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
The most relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE, finding results that our quality-estimation analysis corroborates.
Our work extends theirs in three directions: (i)~structural matching beyond surface-level agreement, (ii)~testing whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection (it does not), and (iii)~a difficulty gradient revealing non-obvious findings---WNUT-17 conditional correlations collapse to $\rho{=}0.038$ (n.s.) and LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$)---that would be invisible on a single dataset.

Structured IE requires schema-compliant output, making constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} the standard inference strategy---without it, a substantial fraction of outputs are unparseable.
All experiments use constrained decoding, the regime under which structured IE is practically deployed.

Our central finding is the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): under constrained decoding, consistency-based signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) but fail at sample selection despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
By construction, four of five signals assign identical scores to all candidates from the same input, precluding per-sample discrimination.
The non-trivial questions are whether (a)~consensus-proximity selection---instantiating MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, freitag2022high, muller2021understanding} with structural utility functions---can recover discrimination, and (b)~whether log-probability, the only per-sample signal, can exploit the headroom.
Both fail: MBR utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); log-probability is severely compressed under constrained decoding (60\% of instances effectively tied), though where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
Our findings are specific to the constrained decoding regime; whether the gap persists under free-form generation remains an open question.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals predict instance-level quality---high agreement correlates with high F1. \textbf{Right}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, precluding sample selection. Consensus-proximity selection does not recover per-sample discrimination.}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting confidence [VC], Soft Jaccard [SJ]), surface (exact match [EM], Fleiss' $\kappa$ [FK]), and model-internal (log-probability [LP])---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.
Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{The correlation-selection gap and its diagnosis.}
    We demonstrate that strong quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$, AUROC${=}0.75$) coexists with selection failure ($p{>}0.39$, 13--18~pp oracle headroom) under constrained decoding.
    Log-probability---the only per-sample signal---fails due to score compression (60\% of instances effectively tied); where compression is mitigated, it becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
    Consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) also fails to bridge the gap.

    \item \textbf{A systematic evaluation framework.}
    We compare five confidence signals from three families---structural, surface, and model-internal---across quality estimation, binary discrimination, and sample selection, showing that these metrics decouple and single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.

    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
    Signal rankings shift with task difficulty: EM leads on easy tasks, SJ on hard tasks---consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
    At the capability boundary (WNUT-17, 52\% zero F1), conditional correlations collapse to non-significance and LP exhibits strong negative correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$), indicating overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs.
    NER findings span three datasets; RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone (preliminary).
\end{enumerate}

This rules out insufficient diversity as an explanation for the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}
The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to greedy within a bound $\delta$.
The $\delta$ values are anchored to oracle headroom (13--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
The breakpoint $\delta^*$---the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST---ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.
On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to greedy (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though exact match leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across tested model families, though with model-dependent magnitude.
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (constrained-decoding compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
Under constrained decoding, LP scores are severely compressed: 60\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---is the primary mechanistic bottleneck, though whether compression fully accounts for the gap remains open.
The LP compression mechanism is a direct consequence of constrained decoding's restricted token space; alternative decoding strategies may yield different LP distributions.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires either per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust} or relaxation of the constrained-decoding regime that compresses LP resolution; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.

\begin{abstract}
Test-time scaling through repeated sampling promises quality gains for LLM-based information extraction (IE), but whether confidence signals can identify the best among multiple outputs remains untested for structured tasks.
Under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---we compare five confidence signals across NER and RE with two 8B-parameter model families.
These signals achieve strong quality estimation (Spearman $\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75), yet none significantly improves sample selection over greedy decoding despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom---a \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
Four of five signals are instance-level by construction and thus cannot rank candidates; the empirically interesting question is whether consensus-based strategies (MBR/proximity) or per-sample signals (log-probability) can bridge this gap.
They cannot: consensus-proximity selection fails because utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them, and log-probability fails because constrained decoding compresses its scores (60\% of instances effectively tied)---though it becomes a significant selector where compression is mitigated ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
These results establish that consistency signals are quality estimators, not output selectors, for structured IE under constrained decoding.
\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
Test-time scaling through repeated sampling promises quality gains for LLM-based information extraction, but whether confidence signals can identify the best output among multiple candidates remains untested for structured tasks.
Under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---we evaluate five confidence signals from three families across NER and relation extraction on three benchmarks with two 8B-parameter model families.
These signals achieve strong quality estimation, yet none significantly improves sample selection over greedy decoding despite 13--18 percentage points of oracle headroom.
Four of five signals are instance-level by construction and cannot rank candidates; the key empirical question is whether log-probability---the sole per-sample signal---or consensus-proximity selection can bridge this gap.
Neither succeeds: log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties for 60\% of instances under constrained decoding, while consensus-proximity (MBR decoding) fails because utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
Where log-probability compression is absent, selection recovers significant gains ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$), identifying constrained-decoding score compression as the primary bottleneck.
Signal rankings further depend on task complexity, with findings consistent across model families.
\end{abstract}

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though exact match leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across tested model families, though with model-dependent magnitude.
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (constrained-decoding compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
Under constrained decoding, LP scores are severely compressed: 60\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression under constrained decoding---the standard regime for schema-compliant IE---is the primary mechanistic bottleneck, though whether compression fully accounts for the gap remains open.
The LP compression mechanism is a direct consequence of constrained decoding's restricted token space; alternative decoding strategies may yield different LP distributions.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires either per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust} or relaxation of the constrained-decoding regime that compresses LP resolution; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.

\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.
+\paragraph{Toward mechanistic confirmation.}
+Our diagnosis predicts that LP score compression should diminish under free-form (unconstrained) generation, where the full token vocabulary is available at each step.

+A controlled ablation---comparing LP selection under constrained versus free-form decoding on identical instances, with post-hoc JSON parsing for the free-form condition---would directly test whether the bottleneck is decoding-regime-specific.

+For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).

Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across tested model families, though with model-dependent magnitude.

\paragraph{Temperature sensitivity.}
SJ NER $\rho$ shifts from 0.388 ($T{=}0.7$) to 0.360 ($T{=}1.0$), a difference of 0.028 whose bootstrap confidence interval includes zero.
FK shows mixed behavior: NER $\rho$ drops by 0.054, while RE $\rho$ increases by 0.091, likely reflecting reduced diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks.
Across all comparisons, the SJ--FK relative ordering is preserved at both temperatures on NER (0.388 vs.\ 0.321 at $T{=}0.7$; 0.360 vs.\ 0.267 at $T{=}1.0$), indicating a stable signal hierarchy despite numerically small temperature effects.

\paragraph{Sample size scaling.}
Increasing from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ improves SJ on Qwen SciERC NER: $\rho$ rises from 0.360 to $0.412{\pm}0.025$ (three seeds: 0.428, 0.424, 0.384), a gain of $+0.052$.
The magnitude of $N$-scaling gains is setting-dependent---LLaMA SciERC NER yields $+0.016$ and Qwen CoNLL NER $+0.014$---though the direction is consistently positive.
LLaMA CoNLL exhibits the most uniform scaling: all four consistency signals gain $\Delta\rho{\approx}{+}0.030$ (range: $+0.027$ to $+0.032$) while LP gains only $+0.003$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}).
FK $N$-scaling is inconsistent: degradation on SciERC ($-0.007$ to $-0.019$) but improvement on CoNLL with LLaMA ($+0.027$), suggesting sensitivity to both model and task characteristics.
VC $N$-scaling is consistently positive ($+0.005$ on Qwen CoNLL, $+0.018$ on LLaMA SciERC, $+0.062$ on Qwen SciERC), while LP is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta{\leq}0.021$).
SJ, EM, and VC scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows setting-dependent variation, suggesting that structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to $N$.

\paragraph{Cross-model transfer.}
LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct replicates the structural-over-surface ordering on SciERC NER (SJ $\rho{=}0.363$, FK $\rho{=}0.327$).
On CoNLL, the gap across model families is minimal (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA) vs.\ 0.436 (Qwen), $\Delta{=}0.005$.
At $N{=}16$, the structural-over-LP advantage holds across all four tested settings: Qwen SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.411$ vs.\ LP 0.259, $\Delta{=}{+}0.152$), Qwen CoNLL (EM $\rho{=}0.463$ vs.\ LP 0.328, $\Delta{=}{+}0.135$), LLaMA SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.452$ vs.\ LP 0.277, $\Delta{=}{+}0.175$), and LLaMA CoNLL 3-seed (SJ $\rho{=}0.463{\pm}0.007$ vs.\ LP $0.310{\pm}0.005$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.153$).

\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
The SJ advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: VC reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, LP $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.

\paragraph{Length vs.\ log-probability.}
Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter} shows that mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$, $n{=}4{,}232$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$, $n{=}3{,}176$), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for LP's selection failure: longer outputs receive \textit{higher}, not lower, token-averaged log-probability under constrained decoding.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_length_logprob_scatter}
\caption{Output length vs.\ mean log-probability on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Positive correlations (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$) rule out length-penalty confounding.}
\label{fig:length_logprob_scatter}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, making the two selection rules equivalent.
Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, confirming that structural advantage is robust across both models and evaluation conditions.
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while LP drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

\paragraph{WNUT-17 full signal analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:wnut} reports all five signals on WNUT-17.
VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$) on the full set, but conditional analysis (non-zero F1 instances) reveals this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary: conditional $\rho{=}0.038$ ($p{=}0.49$).
LP shows the reverse pattern: full-set $\rho{=}{-}0.410$ but conditional $\rho{=}0.350$, the highest among all signals on the conditional set.
This inversion confirms that full-set correlations on high-failure-rate datasets conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.

\paragraph{Cross-configuration selection analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection} extends the selection analysis to four additional configurations.
On LLaMA SciERC, where output diversity remains substantial (18\% identical outputs, 39\% unique), LP achieves the highest selection F1 (0.652) at $N{=}8$ but still falls within bootstrap noise of greedy (0.646), replicating the gap observed on Qwen SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
On CoNLL, 57--88\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples, reflecting a ceiling effect (greedy F1 ${\approx}$0.91--0.92) rather than signal failure; selection analysis on these configurations is uninformative because there is little per-sample variance for any signal to exploit.

Best non-oracle signal per row in \textbf{bold}. No signal significantly outperforms greedy in any configuration; CoNLL shows especially tight clustering where greedy already exceeds 0.90.}
\label{tab:cross_selection}
\begin{tabular}{llccccccc}
\toprule
Config & $n$ & Greedy & Oracle & SJ & FK & EM & LP & VC \\
\midrule
LLaMA/SciERC $N{=}8$ & 529 & .646 & .778 & .643 & .639 & .634 & \textbf{.652} & .633 \\
